kurz: What can be proven about the passive bubble thesis, what cannot, and why concentration in the world index still deserves attention.

bloecke.md:
That index funds have become large is undisputed. What remains open is whether their size distorts the prices that they themselves adopt without checking.

An index fund forms no judgement about a company. It buys the stocks that the index prescribes, in the weight that the index prescribes, and at the prevailing price. A concern can be derived from this. If more and more capital is invested in this way, at some point there will be no one left to check whether prices are right. The argument deserves to be taken seriously. However, it can be tested against data, and in its strong form it does not stand up to this test.

## The argument in its strongest form

The criticism has four components, which are often mixed up even though the evidence for them varies in strength.

The first component is **price formation**. Prices arise when market participants process information and act on it. Index strategies do not do this. The larger their share, the smaller the part of the market that values companies.

The second concerns **market capitalisation weighting**. An index weighted in this way automatically holds more of whatever has become more expensive, because the weight rises with the price. It therefore contains a built-in momentum component that no valuation limits.

The third is the **index effect**. When a stock is added to a large index, all index funds have to buy it regardless of price, and sell it when it is removed. This trading is forced and price-insensitive.

The fourth is feedback. When the heavyweights rise, the index rises. This leads to higher inflows into index products, which in turn buy a disproportionate amount of the heavyweights. This self-reinforcing cycle can run in both directions, that is, downwards as well.

bloecke.md:
In 1980, Sanford Grossman and Joseph Stiglitz showed that a perfectly informationally efficient market is impossible. If all information were already reflected in the price, no one would have an incentive to pay for information. But then the information could not get into the price either. Markets therefore need a paid minority that does research. The majority benefits from this as free riders.

It follows that there is, in theory, an upper limit to the passive share. It does not follow that the market is close to this limit. The incentive to do research grows to the extent that research becomes scarce. This is a self-regulating equilibrium and not a threshold at which the market suddenly fails.

## Holdings and trading

The most common error in the debate is to equate holdings with trading. The fact that index funds hold a lot says nothing about how much they trade. Prices, however, are set by the most recently executed order and not by holdings at rest. Index funds also have extremely low turnover. They buy when money flows in, sell when money flows out and adjust their holdings when the index changes; beyond that, they do not trade.

bloecke.unter: The shares of holdings are estimates from secondary sources and tend to be lower bounds; for price formation, only the shares of trading volume in the lower half count.

bloecke.md:
Depending on the method, estimates of the share of index strategies in trading range between around 1% and 10%. A widely cited Vanguard study from 2019 arrived at about 5%, and ICI, BlackRock and S&P Dow Jones are of the same order of magnitude. This contrasts with a trading volume of which about half consists of high-frequency trading. On top of that come hedge funds, market makers, companies' share buybacks and private investors. On an ordinary trading day, Nvidia's share price is therefore very unlikely to be set by a savings plan.

These figures do not come from primary statistics and only indicate orders of magnitude. However, all surveys consistently show a high share of holdings and a low share of trading.

In 2019, Michael Burry, known for his bet against the US mortgage market, publicly compared passive investing with the structured credit products of the years before 2008. In his view, price formation no longer took place in index funds, and capital was flowing into stocks that nobody valued. Moreover, liquidity would not be sufficient if many investors wanted to exit at the same time. This, he said, applied especially to small, illiquid stocks, where an index fund has to sell when money flows out without a buyer being available.

The comparison fails on one essential point. Structured credit products were leveraged and opaque; an equity index fund is neither. It holds the shares named by the index, publishes its holdings daily and has no debt. When money flows out, it has to sell proportionally. This depresses prices but does not lead to forced liquidations from credit lines.

The thesis also leads to a prediction that can be tested. If index flows systematically distort prices, active managers should find it particularly easy to make money where indexing is most advanced. The opposite is measured. In the Morningstar barometer for mid-2025, the ten-year success rate of active managers in the most heavily indexed segment, US large blend, was 5.8%. In the broad US stock market, according to SPIVA (as of 30 June 2025), 90.3% of active funds failed to beat their benchmark over ten years. Active managers are evidently not finding the mispriced stocks that should exist according to the thesis.

## Decline of the index effect

For a long time, inclusion in a large index was regarded as a sure price gain. In the 1990s, US stocks rose on average by several percentage points around the announcement of their inclusion in the S&P 500. More recent studies, above all the one by Greenwood and Sammon, practically no longer find this effect. Over the course of the 2010s, it shrank to a size that is barely measurable statistically.

This finding directly contradicts the bubble thesis. If forced index trading were a growing force, the inclusion effect would have had to increase. In fact it has decreased, presumably because professional traders now anticipate index inclusions and index providers have toned down their methodology. This suggests that the market has eliminated a known inefficiency.

## Concentration in the world index

One part of the criticism, however, cannot be refuted. At the end of August 2026, the MSCI World consisted of around 1,280 stocks, and the ten largest of them accounted for 26.61% of the index. Nvidia alone accounted for 5.56%, Apple for 5.07, Microsoft for 3.90, Amazon for 2.74 and Alphabet A for 2.15. Depending on the data provider and reporting date, the US share was around 70% to 72%. In the iShares Core S&P 500, the ten largest positions accounted for 37.8% at the end of August 2026; in the S&P 500 in 2010, the figure was around 18% according to secondary sources.

bloecke.titel: Weights in the MSCI World as of 31 Aug 2026
bloecke.unter: The index comprises around 1,280 stocks; just over a quarter of the money invested goes to ten of them.

bloecke.md:
Index funds did not cause this concentration on their own; above all, they reflect it. With market capitalisation weighting, a fund holds each stock at exactly its share of the overall market. If new money flows proportionally into all positions, the relative weights do not shift. The effect is the same as if the whole market became slightly larger. The weights of a few companies have risen mainly because their profits and valuations have risen. Whether inflows into index funds have contributed to this is disputed in research. Jiang, Vayanos and Zheng (Review of Financial Studies, 2025) find that such inflows raise the share prices of the largest companies disproportionately.

This does not make the concentration harmless. It is above all a valuation and diversification risk and at most partly a consequence of indexing. This risk can be quantified.

bloecke.titel: Illustrative calculation of the index loss if the ten largest stocks slump
bloecke.unter: Calculated from the weights (26.61% and 9.47% respectively) on the assumption that all other stocks remain unchanged; not a forecast.

bloecke.md: An index that caps each individual position at 1% arrives at a top 10 weight of around 9.5% instead of 26.6%. The same slump affects it only about one third as much. In return, it deliberately deviates from the market. Investors who choose a capped index are betting against the largest companies and bear higher ongoing charges and turnover costs. This decision is legitimate, but it is an active decision.

bloecke.md:
## Practical implications

The debate does not produce a sell signal. It provides no date, no threshold and no statement about which stocks are mispriced. Taking it as a reason to act means replacing broad diversification with a bet on the right timing, for which the thesis itself offers no basis.

What does make sense is a precise breakdown of your own risk. A world ETF is less diversified than its name suggests. If the risk is to be spread more widely, the options are adding emerging markets and small caps, an equal-weighted or capped index, and a higher bond allocation. All three options cost money or lead to deviations from the market result that you have to be able to bear. They should be decided on as part of your own investment policy and not as a reaction to a headline.

For tax purposes, switching from a world ETF to a capped product is a sale. The gain is determined under Section 19(1) InvStG (Investment Tax Act). For an equity fund that continuously holds more than 50% equity participations (Section 2(6) InvStG), the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) under Section 20(1) InvStG applies. The remainder is subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act) plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge, 26.375% in total. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 per person (Section 20(9) EStG) reduces the tax base.

With a book gain of €20,000, 20,000 × 0.7 = €14,000 is taxable. After deducting the €1,000 allowance, €13,000 remains, on which €3,428.75 in tax is due. This money leaves the portfolio immediately and no longer contributes to performance. However, the tax would also be due on a later sale; the switch brings it forward. The disadvantage therefore consists of the returns that this amount would have earned up to the originally planned sale. Whether this is worthwhile for lower concentration depends on the investment horizon, the size of the gain and the difference in risk between the two products.

The strong form of the bubble thesis fails on the distinction between holdings and trading. Index funds hold a lot and trade little, and prices arise in trading. What remains of the criticism is the high concentration in the world index. It is above all a valuation risk and at most partly a consequence of indexing. Investors need to know this risk and either bear it or reduce it deliberately and at a cost.

A claim is only meaningful if you can state which observations would refute it. For the passive bubble, the following predictions can be tested:

- Active managers should win where indexing is most widespread. So far the opposite is true; success rates are lowest in the most liquid, most heavily indexed segments.
- The index inclusion effect should grow. In fact, it has almost disappeared.
- The dispersion of valuations within the index should decrease systematically, because capital flows proportionally without a view on price. The concentration data show the opposite; valuations are diverging widely.
- Index funds should sell disproportionately in periods of stress and thereby trigger self-reinforcing price falls. So far, if anything, inflows have been observed during downturns, because savings plans continue automatically.

None of these points has been conclusively settled. For a serious test of the thesis, you should watch these four variables and not the fund industry's market share announcements.

mitnehmen: Share of holdings and share of trading are different measures, and in trading, where prices are formed, index strategies account for only a low single-digit to low double-digit percentage.
The Grossman-Stiglitz argument shows that there is a theoretical upper limit to passive investing and that the incentive to do research rises automatically the scarcer research becomes.

Burry's comparison with structured credit products does not hold, because equity index funds are neither leveraged nor opaque, and his prediction that active managers would benefit has not come true so far.

The concentration in the MSCI World, with 26.61% in ten stocks and around 70% in the US, is real and documented, but it mainly reflects market developments and is not due to index funds alone; whether their inflows make the largest stocks even more expensive is disputed.

Switching brings forward the 26.375% tax on the taxable part of the gain, and the returns on this amount are then missing from the portfolio; this disadvantage must be weighed against the benefit of lower concentration.
